subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday March 31, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Rogers-Mr. Sanderson in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance towards the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress, and for such payments out of moneys appropriated by parliament as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of the session I promised I would take an early opportunity to present a detailed survey of the existing relief situation, and review the results obtained under the several measures adopted by the government for the relief of unemployment and agricultural distress. Since that undertaking was given there have been three debates on unemployment, but apart from the debate on the address in reply these discussions occurred on resolutions, and were therefore somewhat restricted in scope. This is the first opportunity I have had to speak generally and at some length on the problem which has become the primary responsibility of the Department of Labour in so far as its federal aspects are concerned. Hon. members will recall that I had intended to make this statement on the second reading of the bill which would be introduced following the approval of the resolution now before us. However, it was the wish of the committee that the resolution should remain in committee and this statement be made during the discussion thereon. That is the present position.
It so happens that it is just over two years since I addressed the house for the first time on the subject of unemployment. The occasion of that discussion was a motion for the second reading of the bill to establish the national employment commission. In July of last year the interim report of the national employment commission was submitted and its publication authorized by the government. During the past week the final report of that commission was tabled and distributed to members. I realize it is the wish of the committee that I should deal with the subject matter of these reports, and particularly the
main recommendations contained in the final report. I propose to do that before I have finished.
As I mentioned a moment ago, two years have passed since I spoke first to hon. members on the question of unemployment. At that time we were all keenly aware of the gravity of the situation that confronted the country, and I sought to deal with the question without any appeal to party prejudice or any resort to recrimination. Let me say at once that I intend to follow the same policy this afternoon. This does not mean that as a government we seek any immunity from criticism where criticism is due. We must be equally ready to give reasons for what we have done and for what we have refrained from doing. We are prepared to do just that. It does mean that after two and a half years in the Department of Labour I have not changed my conviction that the question of economic insecurity, or perhaps I should say the solution of the problem of economic insecurity, transcends all sectional differences, and it certainly transcends the political fortunes of individuals.
Without question it is the most vital problem which confronts all governments at this time, regardless of the measures that may be adopted to deal with it. I should like to suggest to the committee that in its wider aspects it involves our whole theory of government and it raises issues, as I have had occasion to mention before, which lie at the very root of our system of federal public finance. I shall do no more than mention these considerations at this tame, but I shall return to them later in order to emphasize the interrelation of measures which may be adopted to deal with unemployment and other aspects of national policy and constitutional reform.
Before dealing with the work of the national employment commission, I think it will contribute to the information of the committee and place this work in a proper perspective if I deal first with a number of important decisions which were made by this government in relation to unemployment and the relief situation before the national employment commission was established, When we came into office in October, 1935, perhaps the most urgent question that met us was the determination of the grants in aid from the dominion treasury .to the provinces for the relief of unemployment and agricultural distress. We met that problem, following a dominion-provincial conference and following very strong representations made by a conference of Canadian mayors held in Montreal

Relief and Agricultural Distress
at about the same time, by an increase of seventyjfive per cent in the grants in aid payable to the provinces for the relief of unemployment conditions.
I want to speak of that at the present time because it is related to something that I shall have to say a little later. I think it will also be useful if I indicate to hon, members, particularly those who were not here during the last parliament, the train of events which led up to the system of grants in aid to the provinces, which, as I have said, was one of the first problems which confronted us as a government when we came into office. When direct relief was instituted in this country as a result of the abnormal conditions which had developed from 1930 onward, that system of relief was based upon the assumption that in constitutional practice the primary responsibility for dealing with unemployment and distress lay with the municipality, but when it became too great for the municipality it was time for the province to render assistance, and when it became too great for the province and assumed national dimensions, it was time for the dominion government to come to the assistance of the provinces.
That principle, if I might term it such, was expressed very clearly on a number of occasions by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he was Prime Minister, and also by the present Prime Minister when in opposition. I think I cannot do better at the moment than quote the words of the present leader of the opposition as of September 10, 1930, which was about the time when it was considered necessary to institute this system of direct relief through grants in aid from the dominion treasury.

speechtext:
It was not until the
next year that direct relief came into being.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
That is quite true. In the first year resort was had rather to a system of works by which this government assisted the provinces and the municipalities in the execution thereof. With that correction, I quote the words of my right hon. friend:
But this dominion will not be engaging in that form of relief or business which primarily it is the duty of the provinces or municipalities to undertake; but to assist them in the discharge of that duty this grant is being asked for.
I come now to the next year, when on July 23, 1931, the present Prime Minister is reported on pages 4101 and 4102 of Hansard as follows:
It is not wise from the point of view of principle for one government to raise taxes and pass them over to other governments to
IMr. Rogers.]
be expended. The government which raises the taxes ought to control their expenditure. I believe that was the principle laid down at the time of confederation. It was recognized that the provinces would need something in the way of subsidies to supplement their sources of income, but I contend that one of the bases of the confederation act was the idea that the federal and provincial governments would have certain definite fields of services assigned to them, that they should have complete control over those services, that they would raise the moneys necessary and see to their expenditure. If for any reason the division is not fair, then adjustments should be made by the paying of additional or altered subsidies.
Then I come finally to the close of the period during which the leader of the opposition was Prime Minister of this country, in 1935. The following quotation is from Hansard, 1935, page 166:
Mr. Bennett:	It has been common ground
between the right hon. gentleman and myself that the primary obligation with respect to relief under our constitution rests with the small community, whether it be a municipality, a village, a town, or a city.	The second
liability rests with the province that brought those organizations into being, and if the question is of a national character the dominion must assist.
It was in conformity with those views of the relative obligations of the several governmental agencies set up under the federal constitution in respect of relief and distress that a policy of direct relief was built up in this country from 1931 onward. In the beginning that policy was based upon a threeway division of the financial obligation; the dominion government contributed 33J per cent, the province contributed 33) per cent, and the municipality an equal percentage of the total cost of direct relief.
That system continued until August of 1934. In July of that year the present leader of the opposition summoned a dominion-provincial conference, which canvassed very thoroughly the situation which had developed under the system which I have described. I have read very carefully the report of that conference. The report was not published, and I shall not refer to it in any particular other than to say what was later recorded, that under a system where the dominion government committed itself to a percentage of indefinite expenditures, there was a tendency towards waste and a tendency towards laxity of administration, and it was in view of those considerations that the government of that day changed the method of percentage grants in relation to the problem as it existed in each province to a system of monthly grants in aid of fixed sums, these to be paid to the provinces for their assistance in meeting that problem.

speechtext: There was some variation as to amounts.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
My information is that
there was only a slight variation in the amounts paid under the grants in aid agreements. It is quite true, of course, that the administration of my right hon. friend did deal with special emergency situations in the western provinces on a different basis, but I am referring here only to the grants in aid of unemployment and agricultural distress apart from what was done in the drought area. The grants prevailing from August, 1934, up to October, 1935, are as follows- my right hon. friend is correct; there was some alteration in the case of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, but the grants to the other provinces I find are substantially the same:	Prince Edward Island, 81,250; Nova
Scotia, $40,000; New Brunswick, $25,000; Quebec, $500,000; Ontario, $600,000; Manitoba, $135,000; Saskatchewan, $200,000; Alberta, $100,000; British Columbia, $150,000. These were monthly grants in aid. The only changes were in Prince Edward Island, where there was a reduction from $2,125 to $1,250, and in Nova Scotia, from $40,875 to $40,000. That is to say, there were only minor adjustments. These were the grants that remained in force for the period of fifteen months before this government came into office.
When we came into office we summoned a conference of the provinces and asked the provinces to lay fully before us the situation which had existed in the preceding period and to indicate how far they believed that that system had operated injuriously to the structure of municipal and provincial finance. It was manifest at that time-and one must remember the cumulative effect of these things -that some immediate action was necessary on the part of the dominion government to relieve the position of the municipalities. The municipalities themselves complained that under the relief legislation of the preceding period they had in many cases been unable to raise by taxation their portion of what was required, and were now being confronted with the inevitable results of a process of increase of debt due to the funding of relief costs. At all events the situation as it was presented to this government appeared to be
a critical one, and we met it in the manner I have indicated. We increased the grants in aid to the provinces by seventy-five per cent for the winter months, and in the order in council under which that increase in the grants in aid to the provinces was authorized we emphasized that the increase was designed particularly to afford relief to the municipalities.
It is quite true, as has been said before in this chamber, that in certain cases the provincial governments appeared to be reluctant to pass on these increases to the municipalities, but that occurred in only a very few cases, and as a result of communications addressed to the provinces by the Department of Labour we have reason to believe that certainly during the first quarter of the year 1936 the increase in the grants in aid was substantially passed on for the relief of the municipalities.
From that time forward we have by degrees, in conformity with the improvement in general conditions, gradually reduced the grants in aid to the provinces. I am not going to indicate at this time just when those reductions were made and to what provinces they apply. I merely point out that the first act of the government in relation to the relief situation was based upon a clear appreciation of the cumulative effects of relief costs upon junior governments. We did it to meet an immediate emergency during those first winter months, and as the situation gradually improved we as a dominion government have correspondingly reduced our grants in aid to the provinces.
The next question that confronted us as a government was the disposition of the relief camps. I am not going to deal with that subject at great length, but as I said before I think it is important that we should understand fully just what policies have been followed, and why they have been followed, in order that the committee may review the entire situation at this time. The relief camps had been established to meet an emergent situation which had developed as a result of continued drought in the western provinces and of great decline of activity in other industries. As is well known to members of the committee, the industries of logging, lumbering and mining are to some extent seasonal in character, and tend to attract to themselves a large body of fluctuating labour. With drought conditions prevailing in the western provinces it was not possible to absorb that labour in agricultural occupations. As a matter of fact, during successive years there was a steady migration from rural areas to cities.
Relief and Agricultural Distress

The result was a concentration, of transients in our larger cities. It was in the main to meet that situation that the relief camps were established.
When we came into office the relief camps had been in operation for a period of about two and a half years. They were established in every province of Canada with the exception of Prince Edward Island; they totalled in all 144. They stretched across the dominion from Nova Scotia to British Columbia. I think it might be useful to indicate to the house how the strength of these camps increased in the period to which I have referred. As of January, 1933, the number in the relief camps was 1,936; in January, 1934, it was 19,526; in January, 1935, it was 21,631; and in January, 1936, it was 20,241. So the tendency had been for the numbers of these single homeless men, as they were described, to increase during that period, and there was in the nature of things a very considerable pressure upon both the preceding administration and this government when it came into office to increase the number of relief camps in order to provide a refuge for larger numbers of these men.
We had to make a decision as to what should be done with these relief camps. It was announced originally that the administration of these relief camps would be transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Labour. Immediately following that statement, the Department of Labour established a committee of inquiry to visit the camps and to report to the minister with respect to the policy that should be followed in relation to them. The terms of reference to that committee indicate clearly that so far as the Minister of Labour was concerned there was a desire, which of course extended to the government as a whole, to find out whether in the existing circumstances the camps really met effectively the situation created by unemployment and transiency, or whether it would be desirable to close them and deal with the situation in another way.
The terms of reference were as follows:
1.	The desirability of continuing the relief camps on their present basis or in any other form.
2.	The allowance or wage policy which should be followed in the relief camps during their continuance, and the relation of any proposed change in allowance to other forms of unemployment relief, and more particularly to existing schemes for farm placement carried out in cooperation with the provinces.
3.	The adequacy of existing facilities for reestablishing men now in relief camps in industrial and agricultural employment.

4.	The adequacy of existing facilities for general education, occupational training and supervised recreation.
5.	Any other matter in relation to the administration of relief camps which you deem to be of importance in the formulation of the policy of the Department of Labour in relation to these camps.
The members of that committee consisted of Mr. Humphrey Mitchell, formerly a member of this house; Doctor E. W. Bradwin, president of the Frontier college, who has had a long experience in dealing with this type of single homeless men, and Mr. Rigg, the head of the dominion employment service.
The committee lost no time in making its investigation, and upon the basis of its report it was determined by this government that the relief camps would be closed. We stated that we hoped it would be possible to close the camps as of July 1, 1936. Meanwhile, again following the recommendations of the committee, we decided that the allowance of twenty cents a day, which had proved the cause of so much contention and ill-feeling in preceding years, should be altered, that the men in the camps should receive a wage allowance of fifteen dollars a month up to the time of their closing, and that that amount should be paid to them on a deferred pay basis in order that they might be assisted towards absorption in some other line of occupation. It was said at the time that the relief camps could not be closed. It was said that there would be riots. It was said that it would create a disturbance of the labour market, and that, regardless of the conditions which had developed in these camps it was better to continue them than to seek to close them at that time. Fortunately it was found possible, through the cooperation of three departments of this government, the departments of national defence, of transport and of labour, to work out a plan whereby the greater number of men in the relief camps would be transferred to useful and gainful employment on maintenance work on the great railway systems of this country. Special employment officers were also sent to the various camps in order to assist others in them toward other occupations. Many were enabled to return to agricultural occupations.
I should like simply to say at this time that the program as announced was carried out to the letter. There were no riots; there were no disturbances. Some ten thousand of these men went to maintenance work upon the railways, and so were placed in a position to earn money,-for the first time in a number of years, in the case of a vast majority of them. Many found other occupations, and the camps ceased to be an integral part of

Relief and Agricultural Distress
the administration of relief in this country as from dominion day, 1936. I should like to say too that in view of subsequent events, whatever may be said by hon. members as to the wisdom of that policy, it can be said that the policy itself was well timed, and also that those who were in the camps were enabled, by the adoption of other methods of dealing with this situation, to move into much more wholesome occupations. From that time forward, although there have been difficulties from time to time in certain of our larger cities, the problem of the single, homeless men has never attained the serious proportions it had prior to the closing of the relief camps.
The next question which faced us was the determination of the real dimensions of .this problem of relief; the desire on our part to think of that problem not merely in terms of numbers but rather in terms of human need and of the occupational possibilities of those who had been unemployed and on relief for a period of years. So in February, 1936, we arranged, following the recommendations of the do-minion-pTOvincial conference in December of the previous year, to have a special trial registration and classification of the unemployed on relief. That was of very great value in laying a foundation for the more complete and more accurate registration which was conducted subsequently by the national employment commission.
The next decision taken by the government related to the assistance given to the provinces in connection with projects known as relief work. For some years, as I mentioned, the dominion government had assisted the provinces in the construction of highways and to some extent of buildings and .municipal enterprises. The tendency was to concentrate expenditures upon highways and particularly upon sections of the trans-Canada highway which had not yet been built. The result of that policy was that there were in certain provinces, notably in Ontario, large concentrations of single men on these trans-Canada projects, and it was not found practicable to bring to them the heads of families on relief in the larger cities and towns of the province. We believed that it was reasonable in the first place that whatever expenditures were made for relief works should be distributed and located as far as possible in relation to existing employment needs, and we also felt that undoubtedly there would be full support both in this house and in the country for the stipulation in any agreement with the provinces that those working upon such projects should be taken largely from the relief rolls. The stipulation that at least fifty per cent of those working on joint projects should be taken
from the relief rolls was inserted in the relief works agreements with the provinces covering the year 1936-37, and it has continued from then to the present day. We have had the assurance therefore, regardless of the extent of these programs, that they have contributed at least to the reduction of the relief rolls; and we have also had the assurance that the reduction has not been confined to single municipalities or areas but has been distributed as far as possible in relation to employment needs.
Those were the decisions that were taken before the establishment of the national employment commission, and that brings me to the setting up of that body. The second reading of the bill to establish the national employment commission was moved on March 30, 1936, and the commission itself was set up as soon as possible after the bill received royal assent. We made it very clear, when the national employment commission was set up, that we believed that there was a real need for an agency of this kind which could give its attention to certain aspects of this great problem of unemployment relief and also bring about a more effective co-ordination of effort among all governmental agencies having obligations in relation to that problem.
The house will remember perhaps some of the discussion that took place on the provisions of that bill, and it will be recalled in particular that it was emphasized at that time that the functions of the national employment commission were to be advisory. It is true that there is one provision in the bill whereby administrative functions could by order in council be conferred upon the commission; but in the debate it was emphasized by members on the opposite side that it would be undesirable to have administrative functions so conferred, and there was no question as to the feeling of the house that the main functions of the commission should be confined to advising the government with respect to measures to deal with unemployment and agricultural distress.
I should like at this time to refer to the functions of the national employment commission as set out in the act. They are:
The commission shall,
(a)	carry out as soon as possible a national registration and classification of persons on relief in cooperation with the provinces, municipalities and private and public bodies;
(b)	recommend to the minister conditions to be complied with by any province obtaining grants for relief purposes from the government of Canada;

Relief and Agricultural Distress
(c)	recommend to the minister effective means of mobilizing the agencies for relief both state and voluntary, and so coordinating their work as to avoid overlapping and abuses, and to secui'e when necessary, an effective supervision and auditing of expenditures of all moneys;
(d)	investigate and report upon proposals for the carrying out of programs of public works and other projects to aid in providing employment;
(e)	recommend to the minister measures with respect to programs of public works and projects of the dominion, the provinces, the municipalities, and other agencies, intended to aid in providing employment in a manner which will serve to mobilize and coordinate their activities;
(f)	investigate and report to the minister on measures of cooperation with commercial and industrial groups in devising means under which provision may be made for the maintenance and increase of employment;
(g)	investigate and report to the minister upon plans for the establishment of an apprenticeship system in industry;
(h)	investigate and report upon ways and means of providing employment for disabled persons, and cooperate with the veterans' assistance commission in its efforts to secure suitable employment for ex-soldiers;
(i)	recommend to the minister comprehensive measures constituting long-range plans of national development which may be proceeded with or discontinued from time to time as conditions may determine;
(j)	take such steps to ensure publicity as in the opinion of the commission may be necessary to enable it effectively to discharge its powers and duties.
Those were the functions conferred upon the national employment commission, and I will now deal first with the personnel of the commission and secondly with the recommendations which have come from that commission, first in its interim report and subsequently in its final report, which was distributed a few days ago. First may I say this with regard to those who were appointed to the national employment commission and also to the two special advisory committees on youth employment and women's employment. Those who were appointed to the commission and the committees accepted their duties with a very keen sense of the importance of the task and a very keen sense of public obligation. I emphasize that at this time because there have been, and I suppose quite naturally, suggestions occasionally in this house that those who were employed on this work were perhaps not giving to it their full time and that the work might have been concentrated to better effect had there been a smaller commission or had those placed upon these committees been able to give their full time to them. In my own experience with the 
personnel and the machinery of this organization I am fully convinced that we could not have found in Canada a group of men and women more keenly anxious to serve the country in connection with this very great problem.
The national employment commission was organized in June 1936, and the first problems that confronted it were three. I referred a few moments ago to the problem of single homeless men and the measures taken by this administration to abolish relief camps ancf direct those in them to gainful occupations. It was necessary to anticipate the need for caring for single unemployed men and transients in the winter of 1936-37, and the first problem dealt with by the commission was this one, which past experience had proved had in it very serious elements of danger and disturbance. After a very careful study of that problem it was the view of the commission that we could best deal with that situation of transiency and the single unemployed by an expansion of the farm placement plan which had been in operation on a limited scale in previous years. The commission itself arranged conferences with representatives of various provincial governments in order to work out the details of that plan. As a result of the adoption of the plan and the full cooperation of the provinces in it, at least those provinces which felt that the question was a serious one within their borders, the farm improvement and employment plan was set up under which in the winter months of 1936-37 it was found possible to place in Manitoba some ten thousand men and women in farm employment.

The minister's figures in reference to Quebec show that practically four-fifths of those placed on farms during the winter at the expense of the government remained on the farms through the summer.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Has the minister the figures for Ontario?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Although the plan was submitted to Ontario that province did not feel that the situation warranted the adoption of the plan. subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: There were no contributions to Ontario under this plan?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Would the minister give the reasons why the plan was not adopted by Ontario?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: As I recall it the communication was to this effect: it was anticipated that increased logging, lumbering and mining operations in Ontario would very largely absorb the single unemployed, and at the time there was promise of a very marked expansion in those directions. Objection was taken to it also on the ground that the wages paid under this plan, if you can so term the allowances made, were well below what was normally paid farm workers in Ontario, and the department of labour of the province felt that it'would be unwise to adopt the plan in view of those two considerations. I do not think I am misstating the situation as it was at that time.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Could the minister tell us how much was spent on the whole project?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I shall be glad to take note of that question and furnish the information later. I may say, however, that this method of dealing with the problem has been far more economical and, as I mentioned a while ago, in our opinion far more wholesome and far better from the standpoint of the morale of the men and women involved than the former scheme of dealing with single unemployed in relief camps. So far as the expense is concerned, in the last year of their operation the relief camps cost some $9,000,000. On the basis of the increased wage allowance which we introduced in February of 1936 the cost of the camps, had they been continued throughout that year, would have been
812,000,000.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: At the increased rates of pay?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Yes. The increased wages would account for the excess over the 89,000,000 of the previous year. Under the farm employment plan the actual expenditures last year I am quite sure did not exceed $2,500,000, and that amount would also cover the supplementary plans to which I referred, which were in operation in the provinces where the farm employment plan was not in force.
The next problem which was dealt with by the national employment commission was the persistent depression in the building industry. Members of the committee will recall that the employment commission put forward the terms of a plan which actually was put into operation before the house met last year, and which already has had the effect of bringing about a marked stimulus in the building industry. I refer to the home improvement plan. I do not think it is necessary for me to give the details of this plan. It involves encouragement on the part of this government, through the cooperation of financial and loaning institutions, of the repair of private homes. Up to date there has been expended directly under this plan, on home improvements, the sum of 815,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: In a little over a year.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes. The plan is still in operation, and the results under it fully warrant its continuance. At the present time it is in full operation, and we believe there will be still further developments during the coming year.	[DOT]

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Does the minister not mean that the government has loaned $15,000,000, but that the total amount spent would be up to 860,000,000 or $70,000,000.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: No; the loaning institutions have loaned $15,000,000. I was going to say that the experience in the United States, in the operation of a similar plan, has been that for every million dollars loaned directly in this way for the improvement of homes there is an additional expenditure of some $5,000,000, which is induced by what might be described as imitation. That may appear to be an extravagant estimate, but it has been the experience in the United States.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: But the 815,000,000 is the sum total the banks have advanced?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
That is true. About eighty-five per cent of the expenditure is for labour. There is no doubt that the plan has contributed very largely to the improvement of conditions in the building industry. The

advantage comes not only from the extent of the amounts spent, but from the distribution across the dominion. A great deal of it is spent in repairs in smaller municipalities, but I believe the scheme has fully realized our expectations in providing employment in those places in which it is most needed.
Certainly the commission was wise in its decision to deal first with the depression in the building industry. The next question dealt with by the commission was the matter of registration. I have no doubt that by this time hon. members will fully appreciate the advantage of having a continuous registration of the unemployed on relief. Certainly I can say .that from an administrative standpoint there is a tremendous advantage in being able to obtain from the registration branch at any given time a statement regarding the actual relief situation in any district. We can obtain information not merely with respect to the numbers unemployed and on relief, but concerning the occupations from which they came and the facts with regard to ages and other matters of economic and social significance.
Before I have finished I believe I shall have been able to give the committee additional evidence of the value of having this means of continually measuring the fluctuations in the relief problem. A few days ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) directed attention to what he felt were some premonitory signals of a resumption of the depression in Canada. At the present time I shall not do more than say that at least so far as the relief situation is concerned, the figures at our disposal will enable us to measure with reasonable rapidity any changes which may occur from time to time in any part of the country. So far as employment is concerned, although there has been some falling off in recent months, I believe that falling off is certainly not enough at this time to justify our saying that there has been a definite reversal of the upward trend of employment in Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Does that apply to
industry?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I shall deal with that.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Surely the minister knows that the recession in industry is very severe at the present time.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I quite 'appreciate there has been some effect felt-

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Very much.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: -in the border cities of Ontario, particularly,-

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: All over Ontario.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
-of a recession of manufacturing in the United States.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: That is not the point I brought up. I was not speaking about the border cities; I know nothing about them. But I do know that in central Ontario the recession is quite pronounced, and particularly in some industries.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
If the hon. member will permit me to continue, I shall be pleased to deal a little later on with the point he has raised. After all, I quite agree with the hon. member that what we want is the truth. At the same time, while we should avoid excessive optimism, surely we should avoid excessive pessimism.
I come then to the recommendations of the national employment commission with respect to conditions to be attached to the grant in aid. During the first months of its existence the commission advised me, and I think properly, that it did not feel that it should recommend changes in grants in aid until it had had time to make a thorough study of the relief situation. In due course the commission made its recommendations concerning conditions which should be attached to grants in aid, and referred also to the coordination of what might be described as public aid with measures of voluntary aid given by welfare agencies.
The recommendations of the national employment commission were approved in principle by the government shortly after the publication last July of the interim report of the commission. It would have been possible for the federal government at once to have imposed those conditions, as originally recommended by the commission, upon all the provinces. We could have done so upon the basis, I suppose, of refusing to pay any grant in aid to a province unless it accepted the conditions laid down in the report of the commission.
At the same time I felt-and the commission agreed-that it would be desirable that before introducing new conditions with respect to grants in aid we should bring the provinces to us, one by one, and try to secure their willing cooperation in accepting recommendations which were designed to remove abuses in existing relief administration. We did arrange to bring officials of the various provincial departments of welfare to discuss their problems in administration with a committee composed of one representative of the Depart ment of Labour, one from the national employment commission and one from the Department of Finance. Those conferences, conducted with each province, singly, extended over about two months. I did not feel that
time had been wasted. Through those conferences it was found that some of the recommendations of the commission were not uniformly applicable. At all events, as a result of them a draft agreement was drawn up, the two main purposes of which were: (1) to remove the major abuse in connection with relief administration which, in some ways, had put relief in competition with gainful labour, through the tendency in certain places to raise relief scales above prevailing wages, and (2) to secure the cooperation of the provinces in trying to segregate for the time being, for the purpose of information, those on relief who were unemployable and who, therefore, in the strict sense of the term, were not in the category of those who might be directed into gainful occupations.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The minister referred to certain sections of the country where the relief rates were higher than the prevailing rates of wages. To what localities does he refer?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I have not that information immediately before me, and I am not sure that it is desirable at the present time to indicate them. I can say to my hon. friend, however, that in a number of provinces it has been discovered that the relief scales have been raised to a point where they have been competing with prevailing wages. I do not think anyone will seriously argue that that is a desirable situation.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Or that the prevailing rates of wages have been brought down to the relief schedules.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
So far as the prevailing rates of wages are concerned, the article in the agreement makes full allowance for what may be contributed by some other bread-winner who is a member of the family. There was no desire to apply it in a rigorous or inhuman manner; at the same time there was a feeling on the part of the commission, which is referred to explicitly in its report, that an effort should be made to see to it that relief did not compete with gainful occupations. These several agreements were entered into with the provinces after draft agreements had been sent to them for their comments.
I want to emphasize to the committee the fact that in dealing with this whole matter we, as the dominion government, have sought to cooperate with the provincial governments with respect to the administration of relief. Obviously there must come a finality to conferences; obviously there must come a time when the dominion government feels fully justified in saying that there has been enough

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of conferences; that in order to protect its position it is necessary that this or that action shall be taken. But I want to make it perfectly clear that in all that we have sought to do in these last two years, we have endeavoured to secure the cooperation of the provincial governments. We felt also that although it was true that we were merely granting financial assistance to the provinces to deal with the problem of unemployment and distress, the provinces might reasonably expect that we should give something more than grants and make an effort with them to find constructive measures to reduce the problem and to apply measures of effective amelioration.
I come now to the recommendations of the national employment commission which appear in the interim and final reports. Members of the committee who have read the final report will remember that a brief and concise summary of the recommendations contained in the interim report was given on the opening pages. I have touched already upon the main recommendations in the interim report. I have not, however, dealt with one of those recommendations, a recommendation which is given further emphasis in the final report. This refers to low rental housing, and I shall speak upon this matter a little later and in another connection. So far as the three measures that I have mentioned are concerned, I would stress that they have been applied to all the features of the larger problem; that they have been successful in their operation and that they are now being continued.
May I turn now to the recommendations contained in the final report. On page 10 of the final report, following references to these other measures which I have just discussed, the commission directs special attention to the importance of the tourist trade and the possibilities of expansion in that important industry. This question has been referred to at different times in this chamber. According to an estimate by the bureau of statistics, during the past year the tourist industry brought about expenditures amounting to some
S300.000.000. One great advantage of the tourist industry is that it is not one requiring that kind of protection or assistance which tends possibly to place one section of this country against another. No tariff protection is needed to stimulate the tourist industry. Moreover, this industry will confer its benefits upon every section of the dominion, and within those sections benefits are extended to almost every kind of business and occupation, i think the committee will agree generally fMr. Rogers.]
that in stressing the importance of the tourist industry and the possibilities of expansion, the national employment commission has touched upon a matter of great importance and upon a development with great possibilities.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
There is nothing new
in that.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I agree that there is
nothing new in directing attention to the value of the tourist industry. On the other hand, it has a distinct value that we should recognize in its relation to the unemployment situation. In other words, it is an industry capable of encouragement and stimulus in a manner which, as I have just suggested, does not set one part of the country against another.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
How does the minister
determine the value of the tourist business? What is the yardstick?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I shall be glad to get
that information for my hon. friend. The value of this industry has been determined by the bureau of statistics over a number of years. My own feeling has always been that it could not be regarded as more than an estimate. Of course, there is a record of the number of motor cars that cross the boundary at the various points of entry. Estimates are also made of the expenditures of visitors while in the country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: There is a partial record of what they take out.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It is no more than an
estimate, but that does not detract from the value and importance of the industry.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It is a valuable industry.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In connection with the
development of the tourist industry, the national employment commission makes a number of specific recommendations. It suggests what matters should be explored and stresses the importance of close cooperation in this regard between the dominion and provincial governments. The report reads:
The commission submits that the following matters should be explored and advised upon:
National tourist highways,
Retail articles attractive to tourists on which import duties should be adjusted to reduce the sale price,
Historic forts and sites, their restoration and marking.
They refer also to handicrafts, sports and competitive sports projects and so on. So far as the suggestions with respect to the tourist trade are concerned, they have been receiving

Relief and Agricultural Distress
the attention of the government for some time. In their relation to unemployment, they will certainly receive further attention.
During the past two years the government has been working along the line of a broad coordinated program of national development and conservation. I shall have occasion before I have finished to indicate certain lines upon which definite progress has been made within this program. Different features of it have been undertaken by a number of departments of the federal government, either with or without -the joint participation of the provinces. It will be remembered by those who have read the report of the national employment commission that in its reference to public works projects there is a distinct recommendation that as far as possible each government, dominion, provincial and municipal, should deal with its own projects within its own jurisdiction, and that these should be financed and administered independently. With the displacement of joint public works, as recommended by the national employment commission, this program of what I have termed national development and conservation will be furthered by projects which will be controlled and administered within the federal jurisdiction. Within it we propose to give special attention to the proposals of the national employment commission for the encouragement and development of the tourist industry, and this policy has been in its earlier stages, and will !be in its later stages, recognized as an act of faith on the part of this government in the future possibilities of a united Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Has the minister any details of what the plans are for the tourist business?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Before I finish I shall give certain details in connection with what has been done. As the leader of the opposition is aware, specific projects are dealt with normally, have been for some years at any rate, through supplementary estimates for that purpose.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Has the minister in mind cooperation with the Ontario government in its proposed flood control plan?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I do not think I should be or can be inveigled into a commitment of that kind at the present time. I am sure if I answered my hon. friend in the affirmative, there would be no lack of other members who would suggest suitable measures of cooperation in their own constituencies. In the nature of things we have had in recent years to deal
with a vast variety of projects put forward because of their remote relation to unemployment or relief; but my own feeling has been, from the experience I have had during the last two and a half years, that we should concentrate, not on works projects as such merely for the purpose of providing employment, but rather on such projects as will develop this country, conserve its resources and make possible an increasing income, and, I trust, a permanent absorption of a larger number of our people into independent occupations. That has been our policy so far as we could bring it about through the programs which have been undertaken in the past two years. That is the policy we propose to maintain and to extend, and as I said a moment ago I believe it is a policy which will also play its part in counteracting some disintegrating forces which exist in this dominion at the present time. Within federal jurisdiction, under federal control, there are means of developing this country which will not merely contribute to the temporary alleviation of unemployment, though I do not disregard the importance of that, but above all else make it possible for Canada to increase its national income.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Has the minister anything particular in mind in that regard?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I think I shall be able to satisfy my hon. friend. As I have said, there are certain features of this program which are already in operation, and I shall refer to them before I conclude my remarks. There are other features of it which, as I have indicated, may have a special relation to the tourist industry, and which will be announced in due course.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: May I take it that the features to which the minister proposes to refer before he finishes, are those in respect to which the policy of the government for the past two years has been the development of natural resources?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Yes; that and also the means we have followed in stimulating certain of the basic industries of this country in order that they may absorb a larger number of our unemployed. That is substantially what I have in mind.
I come next to the recommendations of the national employment commission with regard to what is termed rehabilitation, or plans for improving employability. In this connection I should like to refer back to another recommendation of the commission which was adopted by the government, and as a result

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of which there has been in operation during the past year a program of youth training through which, I am justified in saying, a new hope has been given to and a stronger morale built up in thousands of unemployed young people from one end of the dominion to the other.
The national employment commission received a report from the youth employment committee, and it passed on to this government a recommendation, based on the report of the youth employment committee, that the government should initiate training projects for unemployed young people. It will be remembered that last year we placed in the estimates an item of $1,000,000 for that purpose. There were some in this house who suggested that that amount was too small; there were others who suggested that it was too large. I think it may be said that the amount, although it might have been doubled with advantage, was perhaps what it ought to have been haying regard to the experimental nature of this work. We lost no time as a government in following the recommendation of the national employment commission in that regard, although I acknowledge freely, as stated in the report of the commission, that so far as the expenditure was concerned, we did not go as far as the commission thought we might have done. Letters were sent to all the provinces in May last, following the prorogation of parliament, asking the provinces to submit to the dominion government projects for training unemployed young people, projects which would have a value in the restoration of physical health and morale, projects which would have what might be termed a recreational value for those who had been unemployed in our larger cities. In other words, we set out in our proposals to the provinces the framework within which these various projects should be made to us, and when those projects were received we dealt with them and adopted them if they fell within the categories laid down by the national employment commission. I am happy to say that every province accepted eventually the proposals with regard to training projects for unemployed young people, and from Prince Edward Island right through to British Columbia these projects have been in operation during recent months.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question in that regard?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I have in mind that perhaps twenty-five to thirty thousand skilled

men-toolmakers, machinists and so forth- have returned to the old country to work in the munitions plants there. What method has the government been following or what has been recommended to train youths between eighteen and twenty-five along these lines? I do not know of any-and I am thoroughly acquainted with many machine shops-who are being trained in these vocations. If we should need them to fill these positions we shall not have them.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The observation of the hon. member-which perhaps is rather an observation than a question-is quite properly made. There is no doubt that there has been an exodus of trained mechanics to Great Britain; but is my hon. friend also aware that in past years we have in the main drawn our trained mechanics from Great Britain?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The technical schools of Ontario are supplying them.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: They are training them to some extent; but I believe the hon. member for Waterloo South will find, if he consults with officials of trades unions and heads of industries, that many of our finest mechanics were drawn from Great Britain. In the last two or three years, in particular, with the great expansion of certain trades, especially the iron and steel industries, in the metal trades, in Great Britain, they have been drawn back to that country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The minister does not intimate that any skilled mechanics of that kind are being drawn from Great Britain to Canada?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Oh, no, not at the present time. The movement is rather the other way. But apprenticeship, as the commission report indicates, falls in the first instance upon industry. That is to say that industry in this country, if it feels it has a lack, either now or in prospect, of trained mechanics, is in its own interest surely under an obligation to take some measures .to train boys who will take the place of those mechanics who, as my hon. friend has said, have gone back to England and of those who are advancing in age and will soon retire. Some of our industries have recognized that problem.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How many young men or young women, as the case may be, have been or are being trained under these agreements with the provinces which the minister has cited?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I have all this information here and I shall be glad to place it before the committee.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What steps are being taken to follow that work up? This training is good. What follow-up is there? If it is not followed up, it is lost.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: First, as to the question put by the hon. member for Kootenay East, these questions are questions which naturally call for an answer, and an answer will be given. I have the information as to the total number who are receiving training, and I propose to give it to the committee. Certainly I have no desire to withhold it.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Why the secrecy now?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The matter of time is surely not so important. I should like to continue along the line that I had intended to follow. But as to the general question which has been put, as I have said, the first obligation for training mechanics lies upon industry. In the second degree that obligation has always rested upon the provinces, which, as this committee is aware, now control the relations between employer and employee, wages and hours and industrial conditions generally. For that reason I want to say frankly to the committee that we as a government did not feel it was desirable, at this stage at any rate, that we should by dominion legislation seek to invade the field of apprenticeship. There have been cases before-and they have been brought to the attention of the house-where the dominion government has by a grant in aid induced provinces-at least they have occasionally told us afterwards that they were induced-more or less, the assumption has been, against their will, into new directions of expenditure. I need only mention agricultural instruction and technical education. Once we have gone into those fields the tendency has always been to make what was designed as a temporary expenditure into a permanent expenditure, and in this way to bring about as it were a transfer of provincial obligations to the dominion by a back-door route, and that has not been a satisfactory method of dealing with the situation.

Would the same
objection not apply to these recreational projects which the dominion is now undertaking?

speechtext:
No, because we have proceeded by way of agreement with the provinces. There has been no dominion legislation dealing with the subject of apprenticeship, which, as I have said, does lie and always has lain within provincial jurisdiction.
So far as these youth training projects are concerned, we have dealt with them by agreements with the provinces. But I would say that, within the categories laid down by the national employment commission, we have sought to get the cooperation of the provinces, particularly the industrial provinces, by bringing about what are termed learnership courses; the learnership courses, while they do not constitute apprenticeship in the ordinary sense of that term, do actually train young men for absorption in private industry; and by our continuing these courses over a period of two years or three years, as the case may be, we are enabled to provide in some measure for this lack of trained young men in some of our larger industries. That is particularly true in Ontario, where more progress has been made in that direction than in some of the other provinces in which, after all, there is not the same diversification of industry or the same opportunity for these learnership courses.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: But surely if it is possible to do that in what are termed learner-ship courses, it would be possible to do it in the case of apprenticeship.

speechtext: I shall not quarrel with my hon. friend over the use of terms. But I shall say this, that, particularly at the present time, I do not think it is advisable that the dominion parliament should assume what might be regarded as legislative jurisdiction over apprenticeship. That is the point I have in mind. We can assist the provinces by agreement as we are doing in connection with training projects.

speechtext: Very wise.

I believe that anyone who has followed the actual results under these grants in aid, which usually have been given under pressure of immediate circumstances without any clear vision of what they may involve in time to come, will agree that that policy is not one which ought to be continued or extended at the present time. Fortunately we have now reached a position where we shall have a review, and I hope a thorough review, of these interrelations between dominion and province under these indirect arrangements through which the dominion has given financial assistance to the provinces to enable provinces to do what they are obliged to do under the constitution but which, in many instances, they are unwilling to concede to any other legislative authority.

speechtext:
Sometimes they concede it, but say they are unable to do it.
Mr. ROGERSSometimes that has been the case; and I think the leader of the opposition will also agree that we are suffering at the present time from the fact that we as a dominion government have been led under stress of circumstances-to meet emergencies, if you will-into making grants to provinces to enable them to maintain administration with respect to great social services, such as old age pensions, to which this dominion government contributes three-fourths of the cost. I do not believe any member of this house can consider that a sound method of conducting federal relations, and it is one which I hope will be rectified. I do not wish to extend that point at this time, having had occasion to deal with it some time ago. If I speak of it now it is because at the Department of Labour more than any other department one is conscious at all times of working in a field of indefinite jurisdiction where responsibilities are not precise and where, for this reason, there is always the possibility of misunderstanding, friction and recrimination. My right hon. friend referred a moment ago to the fact that there had been certain disintegrating influences in this country in the past few years. I am sure that part of that has been due to this very practice of dealing with some of these problems that touch human need upon the basis of dual and therefore indefinite responsibility as among various governmental agencies. It is not a problem that we can settle here at this time; but it is one of which I believe the country as a whole ought to be aware, and certainly we should not continue farther along a way which has been tried and found wanting in the respects that I have mentioned.
I have every desire that stimulus should be given to apprenticeship. There are certain things that can be and are being done by the Department of Labour here to encourage apprenticeship; but my point has been that it would not be desirable for this dominion parliament to assume anything in the nature of jurisdiction with regard to apprenticeship, practically all industrial matters being at the present time under provincial jurisdiction.
The hon. member for Kootenay East asked me if I would be more precise in connection with the projects which have been established under the youth training plan. In the first place it would be useful to give the various schemes that were proposed:
(a)	training projects of an occupational nature devised to increase the employability of young unemployed persons pending employment;

(b)	short term learnership courses, not exceeding one year in duration, devised to provide theoretical training concurrent with specific employment;
(c)	work projects for young unemployed, incorporating reconditioning, training and conservation features undertaken for the purpose of restoring loss of morale among the young unemployed and conserving natural resources.
In connection with forestry work, for instance, the camps that have been established in a number of provinces would be in accord with that classification.
(d)	training projects of a physical nature for young unemployed, to assist in the maintenance of health and morale pending employment.
I have before me in some detail the summary of the training which has been given, and later on I shall be glad to give the results in each of the provinces. The summary goes up to the latest date. I would point out in that connection that a number of provinces in the very nature of things took some time to develop the projects they felt best suited to their needs. It so happens that Ontario and Quebec, the largest industrial provinces, did not actually get into full operation under this plan until October of last year.

I come next to those placed in employment, and that touches a point raised by an hon. member a few moments ago. It was felt by those dealing with this particular problem that the vital need was vocational direction. There is no doubt in the world that the impact of the depression upon the younger men who have come of age in the last few years and have not found work has been unsettling, and the tendency has been to create a kind of hopelessness which requires some sort of continuing direction. I am not going to say that I am satisfied as yet that we have developed a satisfactory system of placement; but we have had it very much in our minds, and we propose to appoint special placement officers in connection with these groups in all provinces and attach them

to the employment offices. We have already made some progress in that direction, but so far as placements are concerned, in this limited time, the figures are *hese: men, 1,371; women, 731. The number of days' work given in forestry and mining, men, was 151,357. Next we come to the rural courses. There were: men, 5,998, and women, 3,427. In forestry there were: men, 2,416; mining, men, 519; physical training, men, 1,671; women, 4,302. The number of those taken off relief were: men, 2,565, and women, 1,173.
That is merely a summary of what might be termed the beginning of a sound enterprise which fully justifies its continuance. I know, from my own contact with some of those who received this training in various provinces, that to them it has meant something more than the reduction of one or two or three from' the relief rolls. It has meant the possibility of receiving training for some definite occupation and has meant a restoration of morale and a new direction towards independence.
